The Runner

Scarlett Thomas

3.24
158 ratings50 reviews
Rate this book
He’s running for his life. And he’s running out of time.

On a sun-soaked Greek island, Jay is on the run. He’s been hunted since he was twenty years old: a contract on his life traded like a commodity, rising and falling with the price of Bitcoin.

Stranded with no passport, loyalty points as his only currency and an assassin in hot pursuit, Jay’s only hope is to escape on a catamaran with a crew on their way to perform an exorcism on a dictator’s private island. When it becomes clear that his shipmates are even more dubious than they first seemed, Jay has to run again – this time into the arms of the beautiful Ellie, who is either his doom or his salvation.

Caught in a web of high-finance, con-artists, the Book of Jonah and ultramarathons, Jay will have to choose between love and survival, and run for his life!

Darkly funny, sexy, exciting, philosophical and enthralling, The Runner is an unmissable literary treat from Britain’s most exciting novelist.

About the author

Scarlett Thomas

34 books1,864 followers
Scarlett Thomas was born in London in 1972. Her widely-acclaimed novels include PopCo, The End of Mr Y and The Seed Collectors. As well as writing literary fiction for adults, she has also written a literary fantasy series for children and a book about writing called Monkeys with Typewriters. Her work has been translated into more than 25 languages.

She has been longlisted for the Orange Prize, shortlisted for the South African Boeke Prize and was once the proud recipient of an Elle Style Award. She is currently Professor of Creative Writing & Contemporary Fiction at the University of Kent in the UK. She lives in a Victorian house near the sea and spends a lot of time reading Chekhov and Katherine Mansfield.

She is currently working on a new novel and various projects for TV.

Ceecee
2,957 reviews2,482 followers
Review of advance copy received from NetGalley
May 10, 2026
Cyprus, May 2025.
Jay is on the run but this is nothing new, it’s been this way since he was 20 and now he’s in his 30s. Currently, he’s stranded, all he has is air mile points, four euro and an assassin on his tail. He takes a job on a catamaran to escape the latest one, but it’s straight into the arms of a very bizarre crew and he’s so he’s off again, this time in Cyprus, where he meets Ellie. Will she be his salvation? Only time will tell. He’s the runner, quite literally and he’s caught in a huge web from which there seems to be no escape. However, we’re off, pat, pat, pat.

Exorcism, assassins, murders, finance, bitcoin, trading air miles, dictators, and running, running, running. Yes, it’s got to be Scarlett Thomas’s latest creation! She always gives her readers something unusual and different and I like that. To start with it feels a bit like being trapped in Hampton Court maze, you’re not sure of your way out or the plot direction but that soon sorts itself out and becomes clear and I settle in for an enjoyable race to the finish.

It’s extremely well written, there’s wit and humour interspersed with the running and Jay‘s backstory. It’s a circuitous route with plenty of good descriptions and a lot of elegant prose. There’s much to keep me entertained, several good plot twists alongside some “intriguing” characters. I never entirely work Ellie out! However, she’s never boring and she has a good heart. I like the way the author has it all play out at the end and everything slots into place. Highly entertaining!

With thanks to NetGalley and especially to Simon and Schuster for the much appreciated early copy in return for an honest review.

Review of advance copy received from Publisher
October 29, 2026
A wild and bizarre rollercoaster ride of cat-and-mouse games, The Runner was a highly original tale of redemption that I blew through in only a handful of hours. You see, it not only oozed wit and humor, but also asked some rather large philosophical questions. That being said, it was more like a fever-dream of a read than a conventional thriller. Hard to find my footing and often downright absurd, the crazy-a** adventures and odd romantic entanglements felt somewhat off to this thriller lover. I can’t put my finger on exactly why, but it just missed the mark for me in spite of the high-stakes conspiracy, clever social commentary, and irreverent dark humor.

What was my biggest turnoff, though? Well, that had to be the misogynistic feel throughout this short and satirical novel. In fact, if I didn’t know better, I would’ve thought it was written by a man. Ultimately, however, my reasons behind why I gave this book the rating I did were twofold. With a plot that felt both jumbled and disjointed and a main character who I really didn’t care for, it was, at times, hard to give a damn about what happened to Jay. Don’t get me wrong, I obviously did or I wouldn’t have finished the book at all.

All of that being said, if you like literary thrillers that are strange and experimental, you just might enjoy this one a bit more than I did. So if this sounds like something you might enjoy, perhaps you should take my review with a rather large pinch of salt. After all, even though it wasn’t really my cup of tea, I still found myself oddly enchanted as I raced through the pages all the way to that abrupt yet shocking last scene. Who knows…maybe I really did just want to find out what happened to Jay. Rating of 2.5 stars.

SYNOPSIS:

Jay has been hunted since he was twenty years old. A contract on his life has been traded like a commodity, rising and falling with Bitcoin for decades. On the run once again with no passport and airmiles as his only currency, Jay will have to choose between love and survival, and run for his life.

While staying at an all-inclusive resort, surviving off of the points he accrued in a previous, more successful life, Jay meets Ellie, a beguiling fellow runner who may even be faster than he is, and is harboring secrets of her own. When an assassin appears poolside, Jay is on the run again, but this time with Ellie, as they find themselves on a catamaran helmed by a sinister and reckless crew.

Thank you Scarlett Thomas and Simon & Schuster for my complimentary copy. All opinions are my own.

PUB DATE: November 17, 2026

Content warning: cursing, sexual content, misogyny, violence, murder

Malcolm
2,073 reviews619 followers
October 10, 2026
What seemed at the outset as a tale of unfortunate coincidence, of perplexing pursuit, and random circumstance turned out to be a carefully and cunningly crafted tale of ubiquitous surveillance, revenge, the Dark Web, excessive materialism (a common trope in Thomas’s work), and redemption (a not so common trope in her work). The story centres on Jay, as he is known – not his birth name, fleeing an assassin, taken in by a crew of sailors who turn out to be exorcists, scamming their way through the gullible wealthy and with get rich schemes aplenty.

Thomas takes this seemingly bizarre set of circumstances as the basis of a tale of redemption, the significance of the con, the subtle and not so subtle dynamics of class, of obsession, greed, and being in the wrong place, all woven into the tale of a man, who for no obvious reason, is pursued by assassins, who may or may not include his travelling companions. She also, and this is a delight of the book, manages to keep Jay – as the pursued – in a balance between perplexity, concealment, and getting on with keeping alive anyway, where an abundance of airpoints is the only sign of his previous standard of living while in the now his focus in on finding, in one case, £165 in cash to provide, perhaps, an option for a way out of his predicament. Along the way, there is running – a lot of it – for release, for hope, for relaxation, and in one case for cash and opportunity in the form of an ultramarathon traversing parts of Kent.

There is a sense of corruption via wealth and alienation it can lead to that is similar to The Sleepwalkers although in this case Jay’s wealth seems a marker of hollowness in his chosen means of escape from his childhood while for others it is either a fantasy or a fatal trap. There is, then, a sense of the immorality of irresponsibility in the book – not in any kind of heavy handed way, but as an ethical underpinning; and I admit I may be over-reading with this.

The shaggy-dog character of wondering where this was taking me kept me engaged, along with a trust in Thomas’s work (based on all I have read of her work) that this was going to take me somewhere interesting, and it did, even if that ‘somewhere’ is left open, in the hands of the fates.

I haven’t heard of this author before but had seen the book recommended and as I’m a fan of thrillers I thought I would give it a try.

The story follows Jay, a guy in his 30s who has been on the run from assassins for 15 years after witnessing a murder and taking evidence.

I found the plot very confusing to follow as it jumped between locations and timelines and bitcoin and blockchain aren’t something I’m familiar with. There was also the religious aspect which confused me as I didn’t know if it was meant to symbolise something or was purely a cover for the scam.

The characters were so flat and two dimensional, I didn’t care about any of them and I think you need to be invested in the characters to keep you turning the pages. For being the main character I didn’t learn much about Jay other than he runs, likes spreadsheets and seems to be weirdly sex obsessed like a teenage boy.

The pacing of the story was very slow for me and that coupled with the jumping about between locations and timelines meant it didn’t really hold my interest. I wouldn’t say the story was thrilling at all. There’s one part on a secret island where it’s a bit like something from a low budget action film but because I didn’t care about the characters it didn’t work for me.

Luckily this is a pretty short book and I appreciate the author has tried to do something different, but for me it didn’t quite work and fell flat.

Thank you to Simon & Schuster for the advanced copy of The Runner!

I really enjoyed this book overall. The concept alone pulled me in: imagine having to literally run for your life and using points to survive. It’s such a fascinating premise.

Without giving anything away, I especially liked the why behind the running. The reason these characters are doing what they’re doing made me stop and think, and I found myself considering the bigger questions the book raises even after I finished reading.

The one part that didn’t completely work for me was the love story between Jay and Ellie. I just never fully bought that they cared about each other as deeply as the story seemed to want me to believe. I wanted to feel more of that connection between them.

And one thing I kept thinking about while reading: I was genuinely surprised this was written by a woman because Jay’s attitude toward women is…let’s just say not exactly flattering. His perspective made for an interesting character, but there were definitely moments when I thought, Scarlett Thomas, are you okay over there?

Overall, though, The Runner was an interesting and surprisingly thought-provoking read, and the premise is one that has definitely stuck with me.

This is a diofficult review to write since I have been a huge Scarlett Thomas fan since her first novel. Unfortunately her stab at a "thriller" doesn't work, coming off as lumpy and fairly uninteresting. The first problem is the Runner himself. I never could empathize with him and, frankly, wondered why I was reading about him. There are sections that are properly fast-paced and full of danger but they are interrupted by a much-too-long attempt at a backstory for the Runner that simply kills the pace; that is the second probem. There are also unaccounted sections where pretty much nothing happens at all. The romance is all rather wan and far too attenuated to land with any punch. As a successful thriller writer myself I know first-hand that writing a literary thriller is supremely difficult. But even for literary thrillers pace is everything, whether it's fast or in say LeCarre's case, slow and methodical, first and foremost the pace must be maintained. If anyone was up to the task it should have been Ms Thomas. Unfortunately, this novel comes up empty.

The Runner was exactly the kind of wild ride i expected it to be!
Jay has spent years perfecting the art of disappearing, but this time he’s really in trouble, stranded, broke, carrying nothing but air miles, a few euros and the small problem of an assassin trying to find him. Naturally, things get even stranger from there.
What follows is a wild, twisty, slightly bonkers adventure filled with criminals, conspiracies, bitcoin, big ideas, and a very questionable collection of characters. It’s dark, funny, clever and completely unpredictable. Jay is exhausted, cynical and a little chaotic, but there’s something strangely endearing about him. Ellie is just as intriguing, and together they make this bizarre story feel surprisingly human.
Scarlett Thomas has created a book that’s equal parts thriller, philosophical rabbit hole, and fever dream. It took me a little while to find my footing, but once I was in, I was hooked. A strange, smart, addictive read that definitely took me somewhere unexpected.

This story is as circuitous and persistent as all the running Jay does throughout the book. I ended up enjoying it quite a bit. Jay was a bit of a twit at times, and Ellie reminded me of several girls I've known over the years, which made the characters feel refreshingly real.
Along the way, Thomas offers some thoughtful observations about society, greed, and the ways people can be selfish and destructive. At the same time, she explores love, trust, and what it means to move beyond the expectations and constructs we're handed. IMHO.
I've seen the mixed reviews, and I can understand why this book won't work for everyone. The pacing has a steady "pat, pat, pat" rhythm that mirrors Jay's running, and it takes a little time to settle into. But once I did, I found it to be an intelligent, thought-provoking, and ultimately captivating read. I'm glad I gave it a chance.
Thank you to NetGalley and Simon & Schuster for the complimentary ARC.

The book is about Jay, a runner, who has been running for his life for the last decade. As Jay runs and hides, we are shown how he lives a life in hiding, which is chaotic, funny, messy, and at times smart. Jay is short on money, living off the grid in an all-inclusive hotel when he meets Ellie. As we come to understand why Jay is running for his life, why the assassins keep showing off, and who is to win once he dies, Jay falls in love (or thinks he does) with Ellie.
As Jay sets out to run an ultramarathon to make $10,000 in cash, we are invited for a crazy ride in which keeping on running is all that matters, and maybe true love?
I enjoyed this book. At times I felt lost a bit, and once I was back on board, the craziness continued. Jay was a complex character, and the chaotic way in which he lives is clearly shown in the narrative. It was a fun read, an exciting read, and if you enjoy messy thrillers sprinkled with romance, then I would recommend this book.

Jay (not his real name) is staying in a Greek resort when he realizes he's been found and is forced on the run with only the clothes on his back. He manages to get a job on a boat to Cyprus, where he continues his clandestine existence of living off of the loyalty points he'd accumulated before a hit was taken out on him years earlier, that has now, thanks to bitcoin, ballooned into an outrageous sum. So, he's comfortable and well-fed, but unable to buy a change of clothes or basic supplies. He does meet a young woman, with whom he quickly forms a casual relationship, but his ties to her are stronger than he knows and he is eventually sucked into a plot to grift money off of the dictator of a small Eurasian country by exorcising the leader's residence of evil spirits. The would-be grifters are inept, helped out in their scheme by Jay's love interest's brother, a defrocked and severely depressed priest.

The plot, if even moderate attention is paid, does not hold together or make sense. It's also very, very weird. As the plot grew more convoluted, it became muddier, eventually leaving me less invested in what happened to Jay, and by leaving the reason for him having had a contract to have him killed taken out on him until late in the book, it was hard to find a reason to care about his fate. Thomas is an imaginative and surprising writer and this book is both, but lacks the cohesion of her previous novels.
